en.text:
Which of the following statements about insurance in aviation sector is/are correct?
1. ‘Aviation Hull Insurance’ covers the physical aircraft, including the body, engine, and on-board equipment.
2. Under the Montreal Convention, adopted in 1999 by over 130 countries, including India, airlines are strictly liable to pay compensation to the family/nominee of every deceased passenger without requiring the family to prove fault.
Select the answer using the code given below:
en.explanation:
Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2. Hull insurance covers the aircraft itself, and the Montreal Convention makes airlines pay for a passenger's death up to a set limit without proof of fault.

  • Statement 1: correct. Aviation hull insurance covers physical loss of or damage to the aircraft itself, including its body, engines and equipment on board; liability insurance covers passengers and third parties.
  • Statement 2: correct. The Montreal Convention of 1999, in force for India since 2009, makes airlines strictly liable for a passenger's death or injury up to 151,880 SDR (since December 2024), with no proof of fault needed.

Aviation insurance has two main parts: hull cover for the aircraft and liability cover for passengers, cargo and third parties. For international flights, the Montreal Convention of 1999 sets a two-tier regime: up to the limit the airline pays for death or injury regardless of fault; above it, the airline is liable unless it proves the damage was not due to its negligence. India applies it through the Carriage by Air Act, 1972, amended in 2009. The Air India AI171 crash at Ahmedabad in June 2025 put these rules in the news.

The trap: (a) is tempting because ordinary damage claims need proof of negligence, but the Montreal Convention makes the airline pay up to the first-tier limit regardless of fault; only claims above that limit can be resisted by proving no negligence.

Read more: International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air (Montreal, 1999); Carriage by Air Act, 1972.

hi.text:

2. वर्ष 1999 में, भारत सहित, 130 से अधिक राष्ट्रों द्वारा अंगीकार किए गए मोंट्रियल कन्वेंशन के अधीन, एयरलाइनें प्रत्येक मृतक यात्री के परिवार/नामिति को, उस परिवार के द्वारा दोष सिद्ध करने की आवश्यकता के बिना ही, क्षतिपूर्ति का भुगतान करने के लिए पूर्णतः उत्तरदायी हैं।

en.text:
Which of the following statements about Crowdfunding is/are correct?
1. Crowdfunding is solicitation of funds (small amount) from multiple investors through a web-based platform or social networking site for a specific project.
2. Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are able to raise funds at lower cost of capital without undergoing rigorous procedures.
Select the answer using the code given below:
en.explanation:
Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2. Both lines come from SEBI's 2014 consultation paper, which defined crowdfunding and listed cheaper, simpler funding for SMEs among its benefits.

  • Statement 1: correct. SEBI's Consultation Paper on Crowdfunding in India (June 2014) defines it as solicitation of small amounts from many investors through a web-based platform or social networking site for a specific project, business venture or social cause.
  • Statement 2: correct. The same paper lists among the benefits of crowdfunding that SMEs can raise funds at a lower cost of capital without going through rigorous procedures.

Crowdfunding pools small sums from many people online. SEBI's 2014 paper describes four models: donation (no return), reward (a product or perk), peer-to-peer lending (loans with interest) and equity (a share in the business). It proposed a framework for security-based crowdfunding as an extra channel of early-stage funding for start-ups and SMEs, balanced against investor protection. Peer-to-peer lending platforms have been regulated by the RBI as NBFC-P2Ps since 2017.

The trap: (a) is tempting because crowdfunding carries risks for investors, but statement 2 speaks of the issuer's side: SEBI noted that SMEs can raise money more cheaply and with fewer procedures this way.

Read more: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Consultation Paper on Crowdfunding in India, June 2014.

With reference to different Committees in India, consider the following details:

Sl. No.CommitteeObjectiveOrganization under which it was formed
1.R.N. Malhotra CommitteeComprehensive reforms of Insurance sector in IndiaInsurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
2.L.C. Gupta CommitteePreparing a roadmap for the introduction of derivatives trading in IndiaSecurities and Exchange Board of India
3.Urjit R. Patel CommitteePreparing a roadmap for reforming bank lending to the Housing sectorReserve Bank of India
4.Y.H. Malegam CommitteePreparing a roadmap for reforms in Microfinance sector in IndiaReserve Bank of India

In which of the above rows are all the details correctly matched?
en.explanation:
Answer: (d) 2 and 4. SEBI's L.C. Gupta Committee prepared derivatives trading and the RBI's Y.H. Malegam Committee studied microfinance; rows 1 and 3 misstate the parent body or the task.

  • Row 1: incorrect. The R.N. Malhotra Committee on insurance reform was set up by the Government of India in 1993; IRDA did not exist then and was created on its advice under the IRDA Act, 1999.
  • Row 2: correct. SEBI set up the L.C. Gupta Committee in 1996 to frame a regulatory framework for derivatives trading; index futures began trading in India in 2000.
  • Row 3: incorrect. The Urjit R. Patel Committee (RBI, 2013-14) was an expert committee to revise and strengthen the monetary policy framework; it recommended CPI inflation as the anchor, not housing loan reform.
  • Row 4: correct. The Y.H. Malegam Committee, a sub-committee of the RBI's Central Board set up in 2010 after the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis, proposed a regulatory framework for microfinance institutions.

Committees are tested by name, purpose and parent body. R.N. Malhotra (1993, Government of India) proposed opening insurance to private firms under an independent regulator, which became IRDA. L.C. Gupta (1996, SEBI) paved the way for derivatives trading. Y.H. Malegam (2010, RBI) led to the NBFC-MFI category for microfinance lenders. Urjit Patel (2013, RBI) recommended flexible inflation targeting with a CPI target of 4 percent plus or minus 2 and a monetary policy committee.

The trap: (c) is tempting because the R.N. Malhotra Committee did reform insurance, but it was set up by the government in 1993, years before IRDA existed; row 3 is wrong too, as Urjit Patel's panel was on monetary policy.

Read more: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy, chapters on the financial market, banking and insurance.

en.text:
Consider the following statements about the Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in India:
1. NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits.
2. All the NBFCs operating in India have to be registered with the RBI.
3. NBFCs form part of the payment and settlement system and can issue cheque drawn on itself.
4. Deposit insurance facility of Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) is not available to the depositors of deposit taking NBFCs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
en.explanation:
Answer: (a) 1 and 4. NBFCs cannot take demand deposits and their depositors get no DICGC cover; some NBFCs are exempt from RBI registration and none can issue cheques.

  • Statement 1: correct. Unlike banks, NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, the deposits repayable on demand such as current account balances.
  • Statement 2: incorrect. Section 45-IA of the RBI Act requires registration, but NBFCs regulated by others are exempt, such as SEBI-registered merchant bankers and stock brokers, IRDAI-registered insurers, Nidhi companies and chit fund companies.
  • Statement 3: incorrect. NBFCs do not form part of the payment and settlement system and cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves; this is a key difference from banks.
  • Statement 4: correct. Deposit insurance from the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) covers bank deposits only; it is not available to depositors of deposit-taking NBFCs.

An NBFC is a company registered under the Companies Act whose principal business is lending, investment, leasing or hire purchase. The RBI lists three key differences from banks: NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, are not part of the payment and settlement system and so cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves, and their depositors get no DICGC insurance. Since October 2022 the RBI regulates NBFCs under a scale-based framework of base, middle, upper and top layers.

The trap: (b) is tempting because Section 45-IA of the RBI Act does require NBFCs to register, but NBFCs regulated by SEBI, IRDAI or other authorities are exempt, and NBFCs cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves.

Read more: Reserve Bank of India (RBI), FAQs, All you wanted to know about NBFCs.

en.text:
Consider the following statements about Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI):
1. MPI is calculated using Alkire-Foster methodology.
2. MPI calculated by NITI Aayog has a total of twelve indicators.
3. Maternal Health and Bank Account are common indicators in the MPI of NITI Aayog and MPI of United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
en.explanation:
Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only. NITI Aayog's index uses the Alkire-Foster method with 12 indicators; maternal health and bank account are its own additions, absent from the global MPI.

  • Statement 1: correct. Both the global MPI of UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) and NITI Aayog's national MPI use the Alkire-Foster method developed at OPHI.
  • Statement 2: correct. NITI Aayog's national MPI has 12 indicators across health, education and standard of living: the global MPI's 10 plus maternal health and bank account.
  • Statement 3: incorrect. Maternal health and bank account are the two indicators NITI Aayog added for India; the UNDP-OPHI global MPI has 10 indicators and includes neither.

The Multidimensional Poverty Index measures overlapping deprivations in health, education and standard of living, each weighted one-third. Under the Alkire-Foster method, a person is poor if deprived in at least one-third of the weighted indicators, and the index combines how many are poor (headcount) with how deprived they are (intensity). NITI Aayog's national MPI, first released in 2021, adds maternal health and bank account to the global MPI's 10 indicators.

The trap: (b) is tempting because both indices share the same method and most indicators, but maternal health and bank account are exactly the two that NITI Aayog added, so they are not common to both.

Read more: NITI Aayog, National Multidimensional Poverty Index: A Progress Review 2023.
